Description: The agent selects simpletest conditions or omits relevant cases, behaviors, outputs, or state variables needed to verify task-required functionality.
Apply When: The verification omits important geometries or meshes, boundary or loading cases, material or solver parameters, temporal regimes, numerical-method branches, or critical outputs or internal state variables; or uses invalid or uninformative setups that fail to exercise required functionality. Apply when the actual test inputs or execution fail to exercise a required regime or behavior, even if the test name or the agent’s description claims that it was tested.
Do not apply when: Do not apply when The agent adequately covers the relevant functionality and outputs but evaluates their correctness using insufficient verification criteria (VF-02 or VF-03).
Example: The agent tests reverse plastic loading and verifies stress and tangent modulus but never checks accumulated plastic strain, leaving a required state update unverified.

Description: The agent relies on broad physical plausibility or mathematical consistency properties that, although meaningful, are insufficient to establish correctness of the task-specific formulation or numerical solution.
Apply When: The agent treats an expected sign, trend, scaling relation, symmetry, conservation-like property, or generic interpolation property as sufficient evidence of correctness, without adequate task-specific validation.
Do not apply when: Do not apply when the primary verification deficiency is the omission of a specific required test configuration, output, state variable, or portion of the computed response (VF-01). Do not apply merely because generic consistency checks accompany other verification activities, or when the agent uses non-independent reference comparisons (VF-04) or ineffective assertions (VF-03) that better explain the same failure.
Example: The agent checks that doubling the applied force doubles displacement but never verifies whether the displacement magnitude is correct. The agent checks wether the values are finite.

Description: The agent uses assertions or numerical acceptance criteria that are logically ineffective to discriminate meaningful errors in the functionality being verified.
Apply When: An assertion is tautological or has a hugely permissive tolerance.
Do not apply when:
Do not apply when an assertion meaningfully tests its intended behavior, even if it only checks a general scientific property (VF-02).
The agent checks boundary, initial, or loading conditions, or prescribed values, even if enforced directly by the implementation.
The verification omits relevant outputs, nontrivial test cases, or scientific behaviors (VF-01).
A valid assertion checks only a limited property, such as abs(reaction) > 0, without establishing full scientific correctness (VF-02).
The agent loosely interprets an informative numerical comparison without a demonstrably defective acceptance criterion (VF-02).
The comparison is circular or non-independent, unless the assertion has a separate defect (VF-04).
The agent modifies a failing assertion to accommodate an incorrect implementation (VF-05).
Example: Agent permits 100 percent relative error, assert relative_error < 1.0.

Description: The agent verifies its implementation against expected results or reference calculations that reproduce the same unvalidated assumptions, formulations, or implementation errors, preventing the comparison from independently establishing correctness.
Apply When: The trajectory shows a self-derived expected value or supposed reference implementation that reproduces the same erroneous or unvalidated scientific or numerical logic as the submitted code, so their agreement cannot validate that shared logic. Apply only when the comparison shares an identifiable assumption, formulation, or implementation error relevant to the failure.
Do not apply when: Do not apply when the reference or expected result is sufficiently independent for the property being checked. Do not apply when only a broad physical property is checked without a reference/oracle comparison (VF-02). Do not assign solely because the submitted implementation is incorrect, or because two valid implementations share governing equations. If an existing test was changed to duplicate incorrect outputs after failure, use VF-05 for the accommodation behavior.
Example: The agent implements an incorrect stiffness matrix and verifies its solver against a separately written reference that uses the same incorrect matrix, obtaining agreement despite both being wrong.

Description: The agent changes tests, expected results, acceptance criteria, or implementation behavior, or the interpretation of test evidence to obtain or justify passing results without resolving the underlying task-relevant discrepancy.
Apply When: Following failing or contradictory test feedback, the agent removes or weakens meaningful assertions, substitutes expected results derived from incorrect outputs, hardcodes a test-specific answer, or otherwise tailors tests, code, or the interpretation of test evidence to justify acceptance without resolving the underlying task-relevant discrepancy. This accommodation may occur entirely in prose, without modifying executable tests.
Do not apply when: The agent legitimately repairs a flawed test, corrects an incorrect interpretation of test evidence, or makes a general, correct implementation change while preserving the intended requirements. Do not assign simply because the agent modifies code after a failed test or revises its scientific reasoning in response to new evidence. For assertions that are inherently ineffective, use VF-03; for circular or non-independent verification not introduced as test accommodation, use VF-04.
Example: After a correct analytical stress expectation fails, the agent replaces it with an expected value calculated from its own incorrect constitutive update, causing the revised test to pass.

Description: The agent makes a functional change after testing and submits the modified code without performing relevant verification on the submitted version.
Apply When: The trajectory shows testing of one version, a later change affecting required behavior, and submission without rerunning checks relevant to that modification; earlier tests need not have passed.
Do not apply when: Relevant verification is rerun after the final functional change, the change is cosmetic, or no test preceded the modification. Do not assign because code differs from an earlier plan without evidence of a code modification after testing. An intermediate unverified edit that was subsequently verified does not qualify.
Example: The agent tests a solver, changes its state-update equation, and submits the edited implementation without running another relevant test.

Description: The agent submits its implementation without performing observable verification activities intended to assess its correctness.
Apply When: The available complete trajectory shows no executed checks, manually performed comparisons, or other actual verification activities before submission; proposed but unexecuted tests do not count.
Do not apply when: The agent performs any observable attempt to verify the implementation, even if superficial or inadequate (use VF categories as appropriate). Do not infer absence of verification from truncated or missing trajectory records.
Example: The agent writes a solver, describes tests it plans to run, then submits without executing tests or performing any other correctness checks.

Description: An identifiable, task-relevant failure in the agent’s verification or debugging process that is not adequately captured by the predefined categories.
Apply When: A distinct observable verification or debugging failure remains unresolved or contributes to the final unsuccessful submission, and none of VF-01 through VF-07 or NV adequately characterizes it. Explain the behavior and supporting evidence in the judge rationale.
Do not apply when: Do not apply when an existing category covers the behavior, Do not assign solely for a scientific error, instruction violation, algorithm substitution, or submission defect. Identify a distinct verification-process failure not captured by existing codes. Do not use solely because the evaluator reports an incorrect result or the cause of failure is unknown.
